title: Pattern recognition: reading a problem for its signals
summary: Map the words and constraints in a prompt to a small set of DSA patterns, then confirm the fit before you code: sorted input, contiguous ranges, next greater, top k, dependencies, choices.
principle: Most interview problems are a known pattern in disguise. Read the prompt for **signals** (input shape, what is asked for, the size of n), name two or three candidate patterns, check each against the constraints, and only then commit. A pattern is a hypothesis you test, not a keyword you match.
why:
Under time pressure the slow part is not typing, it is choosing an approach. Candidates who stall usually jump straight to code or freeze on a blank page. A short list of signal → pattern pairs gives you a starting point within the first minute, and the constraint on n tells you how fast that pattern has to be.

The signals are concrete. **Sorted** input or a monotonic yes/no question suggests two pointers or binary search. A **contiguous** subarray or substring suggests a sliding window or prefix sums. "Next greater" or "previous smaller" suggests a monotonic stack. "Top k" or "k-th largest" suggests a heap of size k. Tasks with **prerequisites** suggest a topological sort. "All combinations" or "all arrangements" suggests backtracking. If you only need the best or the count, and the same sub-choices repeat, that is dynamic programming.

The second half of the skill is rejecting a pattern quickly. A sliding window needs a condition that only gets worse as the window grows, which negative numbers can break. Greedy needs an exchange argument. Saying why a pattern does **not** fit is as convincing to an interviewer as finding the one that does.

diagrams.title: From prompt signals to a candidate pattern
diagrams.alt: Decision flow. A column of yes/no checks runs top to bottom: sorted input, subarray or substring, next greater, top k, prerequisite order, and a sequence of choices. Each yes branch points right to a pattern: two pointers or binary search, sliding window or prefix sums, monotonic stack, heap of size k, topological sort, and backtracking. Backtracking leads to a further check, only best or count needed, which points to dynamic programming.
diagrams.caption: Ask the cheap questions first. Each yes is a hypothesis to check against the constraints, not a final answer.

steps.text: Sorted input (or an answer that flips from no to yes as a value grows) is the strongest signal there is. Two pointers walk inward in O(n); binary search halves the range in O(log n).

"Longest/shortest subarray or substring such that…" points to a sliding window when the condition only gets worse as the window grows. If values can be negative, switch to prefix sums with a hash map.
"Next greater element", "days until warmer" and "largest rectangle" all ask for the nearest element that beats the current one. A stack that stays monotonic answers each in amortised O(1).
"Top k", "k closest" or "k-th largest" rarely needs a full sort. A heap capped at size k gives O(n log k) and handles streams.
Prerequisites, build steps or course orders form a directed graph. Topological sort gives a valid order and detects a cycle when no order exists.
"All subsets", "all permutations" or "place n queens" asks you to enumerate a sequence of choices. Backtracking builds one choice at a time and undoes it; prune branches that cannot succeed.
If you need only the best value or the number of ways, not the list, and the same remaining sub-problem shows up from different paths, memoise it. That is dynamic programming.

diagrams.title: Pair sum in a sorted array: brute force vs two pointers
diagrams.alt: Side-by-side comparison. On the left, brute force tries every pair with two nested loops, about n squared over two checks, and ignores that the array is sorted. On the right, two pointers start at both ends; if the sum is too small the left pointer moves right, if too large the right pointer moves left, so each step discards one element and the scan finishes in at most n steps.
diagrams.caption: The brute force never uses the word "sorted". The pattern exists to exploit exactly that signal.

after.label: Two pointers: discard one per step

diagrams.title: Work at n = 100,000 for each growth rate
diagrams.alt: Bar chart of operation counts at n equals 100,000, in millions. A full n squared grid is 10,000 million. All pairs i less than j is about 5,000 million. n log n is about 1.7 million. A single pass of n is 0.1 million.
diagrams.caption: Real arithmetic: n^2 = 10^10, n(n-1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10^9, n log2 n ≈ 1.66 × 10^6, n = 10^5. At roughly 10^8 simple steps a second, only the last two finish in time.

diagrams.title: Common patterns: typical time cost vs effort to get right
diagrams.alt: Trade-off chart with typical time cost on the vertical axis and implementation difficulty on the horizontal axis. A hash map is easy and linear. Two pointers and sliding window are linear and moderately easy. Binary search is very fast but fiddly at the boundaries. A heap is n log k with moderate effort. Dynamic programming is polynomial but harder to get right. Brute force is easy but slow, and backtracking is exponential and moderately hard.
diagrams.caption: Positions are rough and depend on the problem. The point: the fast patterns are not the hardest to write; boundaries and state design are where the effort goes.

examples.title: Use the "sorted" signal instead of trying every pair

bad.label: Nested loops ignore the ordering: O(n^2)

good.label: Two pointers from both ends: O(n), O(1) space

examples.why: Because the array is sorted, a sum that is too small can only grow by moving `lo` right, so `a[lo]` can be discarded for good. Each step removes one candidate, giving at most n steps. Say that invariant out loud; it is the proof.

examples.title: "Next greater" is a monotonic stack, not a rescan

bad.label: Scan right from every index: O(n^2) worst case

good.label: Keep unanswered indexes on a decreasing stack: O(n)

examples.why: Every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner `while` costs O(n) in total even though it is nested. The signal was the word "next" combined with a comparison.

checklist: Restate the input shape: sorted or not, contiguous range or any subset, graph or grid, stream or fixed array.
Read the bound on n and turn it into a target complexity before choosing a pattern.
Name two or three candidate patterns and say why each fits or does not.
Check the pattern's precondition: monotonic condition for a sliding window, non-negative values for a sum window, sorted order for two pointers, acyclic graph for a topological order.
Write the invariant of the chosen pattern in one sentence before coding ("everything left of lo is too small").
If the output is "all" solutions, expect exponential output size; if it is "best" or "count", look for overlapping sub-problems and DP.
Start from the brute force out loud, then say which repeated work the pattern removes.

antipatterns.title: Sliding window on a sum when values can be negative

bad.label: Shrink while sum > k: misses windows with negatives

better.label: Prefix sums with a hash map: O(n), any sign

antipatterns.why: A window works only when growing it can never make a bad window good again. With negative numbers, adding an element can lower the sum, so shrinking from the left throws away valid answers. The "contiguous" signal was right; the precondition was not.

antipatterns.title: Sorting because you saw "pairs", then losing the indexes

bad.label: Sort an unsorted array, return positions in the sorted copy

better.label: Unsorted + indexes wanted: hash map of value -> index

antipatterns.why: Two pointers needs sorted input. Sorting costs O(n log n) and destroys the original positions unless you carry them along. When the input is unsorted and the answer is positions, the hash-map complement is the simpler and faster fit.

antipatterns.title: Reaching for DP before checking a simpler pattern

bad.label: Jump straight to a 2-D table
bad.code:
"Max sum of a window of exactly k elements"
-> dp[i][j] = best using first i items with j taken ...
   O(n·k) time and memory, hard to explain

better.label: Fixed-size window: add one, drop one
better.code:
sum of first k; then for each i >= k:
  sum += a[i] - a[i - k]; best = max(best, sum)
   O(n) time, O(1) space

antipatterns.why: DP is powerful but costly to design and to explain. Rule out the cheaper patterns first; a contiguous, fixed-size range is a window, not a DP.

interview: In the first minute, say the signals you see: "The array is sorted and n is up to 10^5, so I am aiming for O(n) or O(n log n); two pointers or binary search look promising."
State the brute force and its cost before the pattern, then name the repeated work the pattern removes.
When you reject a pattern, say why: "A sliding window will not work here because values can be negative." That shows judgment, not just recall.
Say the invariant of your pattern aloud (what is true about the window, the stack or the pointers) and keep it on screen as a comment.
At SSE level, mention the follow-up: does the pattern still work for a stream, for data that does not fit in memory, or when k is close to n?

quiz.question: "Find the longest substring with at most two distinct characters." Which pattern fits best?
choices: Sliding window with a character count map
Binary search on the answer with no extra structure
Topological sort
Backtracking over all substrings
quiz.explain: Contiguous range plus a condition (distinct count ≤ 2) that only gets worse as the window grows is the textbook sliding window. Each character enters and leaves the window once, so it runs in O(n).

quiz.question: For each day's temperature, return how many days until a warmer one. What is the key signal?
choices: The output has one value per day
"Next" element that is greater than the current one
Temperatures are integers
The answer can be zero
quiz.explain: "Nearest later element that beats me" is the monotonic-stack signal. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n) instead of O(n^2) rescans.

quiz.question: You need the 10 most frequent words in a stream of 10^8 words with many distinct values. Which approach fits?
choices: Sort all words alphabetically
Count with a hash map, then keep a min-heap of size 10
Two pointers over the stream
A full DP table
quiz.explain: Counting is a hash map; "top k" is a heap capped at k. Keeping a size-10 min-heap costs O(m log 10) for m distinct words, far cheaper than sorting all of them.

quiz.question: Which pair of properties suggests dynamic programming?
choices: Sorted input and a target sum
Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
A directed graph with no cycles
A contiguous range and a fixed size k
quiz.explain: DP pays off when the best answer is built from best answers to smaller problems and those smaller problems recur. Without overlap, plain recursion or divide and conquer is enough.

quiz.question: Why does a sum-based sliding window fail when the array contains negative numbers?
choices: Negative numbers overflow
Growing the window can lower the sum, so shrinking may discard valid windows
JavaScript cannot compare negative numbers
The window must always have size k
quiz.explain: The window relies on monotonicity: once a window is too big, every larger window with the same left end is too. Negatives break that, so use prefix sums with a hash map instead.

practice.prompt: Given an array of integers (positive, negative or zero) and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. n can be up to 2 × 10^5. Talk through how you pick the approach.
practice.answer: Signals: "contiguous subarray" suggests a sliding window or prefix sums; n up to 2 × 10^5 rules out the O(n^2) brute force over all (i, j) pairs (about 2 × 10^10 pairs). A sliding window needs the sum to grow monotonically with the window, which negative numbers break, so reject it. Use prefix sums: the sum of a[i+1..j] is P[j] − P[i], so for each j count earlier prefixes equal to P[j] − k. Keep a hash map from prefix sum to how many times it has appeared, seeded with {0: 1} for subarrays that start at index 0. One pass: add a[j] to the running prefix, add map[prefix − k] to the count, then increment map[prefix]. O(n) time on average, O(n) space. Test: [1, −1, 1] with k = 1 gives 3; an empty array gives 0; all zeros with k = 0 gives n(n+1)/2.
rubric: Names the signals (contiguous, sign of values, size of n) before choosing
States the brute force and why it is too slow for the given n
Explicitly rejects the sliding window because of negative values
Uses prefix sums with a hash map, including the {0: 1} seed
Gives O(n) time and O(n) space with the hash-map average-case caveat
Tests with a negative case and an empty or all-zero case
